paper.title: Language Generation with Infinite Contamination
paper.summary: An indexed membership-query program tolerates finite contamination. The semantic constructions cover set and element density, identification under bounded displacement, and the finite-class noise threshold. The printed Theorem 7.7 has a formal refutation and a separate corrected obstruction.

formalization_scope.summary: All selected results have proofs under the documented interfaces except the literal Theorem 7.7, which Lean refutes. Its corrected version holds for all real displacement factors at least one.
specializations: Theorems 5.1, 5.4, 6.1, 6.5, 6.11, 6.14, and 7.8 are packaged for a collection supplied by an explicit countable enumeration.
Theorems 6.15--6.16 make the common-order assumptions explicit; Theorem 6.18 constructs canonical orderings and proves density invariance under finite target changes.

Corollary 4.5 gives a terminating finite-query oracle program. Other generation and density existence results use classical finite-history generators. Density characterizations use positive requested density.
gaps: For k ≥ 2 no injective stream can have both eventual noise at most 1/k and displacement at most 1/k. Theorem 7.7 with the printed displacement constant therefore has zero literal coverage.

source_assessment.notes: The source uses a density-zero schedule to make the larger language a vanishing-noise presentation of the sparse sublanguage.

formalization.notes: A common full-coverage stream forces upper element density zero on the larger target whenever the generator succeeds on the smaller target.

claims.title: Bounded displacement does not restore identification
claims.statement_summary: A countable collection exists for which identification in the limit is impossible even when every presentation is M-bounded for any fixed M greater than one.

source_assessment.notes: The diagonal stream differs from canonical order by at most one position and therefore works for every M > 1.

formalization.notes: A single family of the naturals and their one-point deletions defeats every finite-history identifier on exact bounded presentations for every M > 1.

claims.title: Constant-rate noise remains fatal under bounded displacement
claims.statement_summary: The printed theorem claims a worst-case obstruction at both noise rate 1/k and displacement factor 1/k for k ≥ 2.

source_assessment.notes: At a sufficiently large odd prefix of length 2B+1, the displacement condition permits at most B true observations and the noise condition permits at most B erroneous observations. No injective stream can satisfy both.

formalization.notes: The literal impossibility is false. Lean proves the adversary class empty and separately proves a corrected obstruction for all M ≥ 1, including the factor in Example 7.2.

lean_links.notes: No stream satisfies the printed joint assumptions.
A family of k distinct languages has a common hard stream for every M ≥ 1.

relations.notes: Theorem 7.7 reuses the finite constant-noise hardness mechanism under an additional displacement restriction.

claims.title: The set-based upper-density bound under M-bounded displacement is one over M
claims.statement_summary: For every real M ≥ 1 there is an adversarial two-language instance on which a uniformly correct generator has upper set density at most 1/M.

source_assessment.notes: The printed construction uses integer multiples. The Lean proof handles all real M ≥ 1 with a floor-increment set, and uses a proper cofinite target at M = 1.

formalization.notes: Two targets share a full vanishing-noise stream with displacement bounded by real M ≥ 1. Success on the smaller target bounds the set upper density on the larger by 1/M.

claims.title: Algorithm 10 generates under vanishing noise and infinite omissions
claims.statement_summary: For every countable language collection, Algorithm 10 generates in the limit from repetition-free presentations with vanishing noise and arbitrary infinite omissions, without the stable-prefix priority used by Algorithm 4.

source_assessment.notes: This is an alternate implementation of the guarantee in Theorem 5.1, retained because it removes the stable-prefix priority mechanism.

formalization.notes: Algorithm 10 selects the longest active prefix with infinite intersection. The resulting fresh-element generator tolerates vanishing noise and arbitrary omissions.

lean_links.notes: Algorithm 10 selects the longest active prefix with infinite intersection. The resulting fresh-element generator tolerates vanishing noise and arbitrary omissions.

claims.title: Finite k-language classes have a one-over-k noise threshold
claims.statement_summary: For k at least two, every k-language class is generatable below noise rate 1/k, while the paper claims a k-language counterexample at and above 1/k.

source_assessment.notes: The periodic example in the printed necessity argument overshoots 1/k on some prefixes. Adding k initial common words repairs the construction and gives a pointwise bound at every prefix.

formalization.notes: The sharp threshold includes impossibility at equality. An initial common prefix keeps every empirical noise fraction at most 1/k; below the threshold a rate-independent generator succeeds.

lean_links.notes: The sharp threshold includes impossibility at equality. An initial common prefix keeps every empirical noise fraction at most 1/k; below the threshold a rate-independent generator succeeds.
The same generator works for every limiting rate strictly below 1/k.

relations.notes: Specializes the general constant-noise characterization to all finite classes of a fixed cardinality.
